title: DuPont Analysis
subtitle: ROE = Net Margin × Asset Turnover × Equity Multiplier
openingQuestion: What does DuPont Analysis break ROE into?
openingOptions: Revenue, tax and cash flow for the period
explanation: DuPont analysis splits ROE into three terms: net profit margin, asset turnover and the equity multiplier. Its value is that two companies with the same ROE can be standing on three completely different legs - retail gets there on fast turnover, luxury gets there on a fat margin, and a third company may simply be borrowing heavily. Knowing which leg the ROE stands on is knowing which shock will knock it over.

realWorldExample.company: Three roads to the same 20% ROE
realWorldExample.description: A typical supermarket chain reaches a high ROE through very large asset turnover even though its margin is only a few percent - it sells a great deal and earns thin profit on each unit. A luxury goods company reaches the same ROE the opposite way: a very fat profit margin and slow turnover. A third company reaches a comparable ROE mainly through a high equity multiplier - thin margin, average turnover, but equity makes up only a small slice of its funding. These three models respond in completely different ways when rates rise or demand falls, even though a league table sorted by ROE shows them as equals.

quiz.question: If ROE rises mainly because of the equity multiplier, what should you be wary of?
options: Financial leverage is running higher
Revenue has been declining year after year
The effective tax rate is coming down
Net profit margin is rising sharply
quiz.explanation: ROE that climbs because the equity multiplier climbed is ROE bought with debt rather than earned by the business, so it is not automatically good quality growth. Falling revenue would drag ROE down, not push it up. A lower effective tax rate and a fatter net margin both land in the margin term instead, and neither of them is a warning sign - they are the components you want to see doing the work. Leverage is the one term that flatters the ratio while making the company more fragile to a rate rise.

quiz.question: Company A has a 20% ROE mainly from a high net margin (strong profitability). Company B also has a 20% ROE, but mainly from a high equity multiplier (heavy borrowing). Which is usually seen as the more sustainable quality of growth?
options: Company A, because its return comes from real operating efficiency
You cannot compare them without knowing each company's industry
Both are equal in quality because their ROE figures are identical
Company B, because leverage lets it grow faster than A can
quiz.explanation: DuPont shows that a high ROE built on margin - real operating efficiency - is usually more durable than a high ROE built on financial leverage. The company leaning on debt is more exposed when rates rise or revenue softens, even though the reported ROE looks identical. Industry does shape what a normal margin is, but it does not stop you comparing the composition of two ROEs. And leverage speeding up growth is precisely the mechanism that makes B fragile, not a reason to prefer it.

quiz.question: A company's ROE has held steady at 18% for five years, but its profit margin has been drifting down while its equity multiplier has been drifting up. What does that mean?
options: The business is improving how efficiently it uses shareholder equity
Operating performance is weakening, offset by borrowing more
The business is shifting toward a very high asset turnover model
Nothing to worry about since ROE has held at 18% for five years
quiz.explanation: This is exactly the information a headline ROE hides. The same ROE with a deteriorating composition means both earnings quality and resilience have fallen. Equity is being used less efficiently, not more - the multiplier rose because there is proportionally less equity behind the same assets. Nothing in the trend points to a turnover-led model, since turnover is the one term that has not moved. And the stability of the 18% is what makes it dangerous rather than reassuring.

quiz.question: A retailer has a 2% profit margin but a 20% ROE. What is that mainly down to?
options: Low interest costs won by negotiating hard with its banks
A preferential tax rate reserved for domestic retail chains
A high gross margin offsetting a thin net margin
Very high asset turnover, possibly with leverage on top
quiz.explanation: Retail lives on cycling inventory very fast: thin profit per unit but a large number of turns, which still produces a high return on equity. Interest costs and tax rates both act inside the 2% net margin that has already been given, so neither can explain the gap. And a high gross margin cannot be the answer either, since gross margin only matters here to the extent it survives down to the net margin - which it did not.

quiz.question: Retail and luxury goods can share the same ROE while getting there by two different routes. Which two?
options: Retail runs on fast asset turnover, luxury runs on a high profit margin
Retail runs on a high profit margin, luxury on fast turnover
Both run on financial leverage, differing only in loan rates
Retail runs on leverage, luxury on a very large asset base
quiz.explanation: DuPont splits ROE into margin, turnover and leverage, so it shows how two completely different models can produce the same number. The reversed version has it backwards: a supermarket cannot charge a luxury margin, and a luxury house cannot cycle its inventory that fast. Leverage is not what separates them either - both can carry debt. Knowing which leg a business stands on tells you which shock will knock it over.

keyTakeaways: DuPont tells you where ROE comes from
Margin, turnover and leverage all play a part
A high ROE is not necessarily a healthy ROE

summary.keyIdea: DuPont tells you where ROE comes from
summary.commonMistake: Easy to miss: margin, turnover and leverage all play a part
summary.action: A high ROE is not necessarily a healthy ROE

sections.text: Two companies with the same 20% ROE - but that number can come from completely different sources, and DuPont Analysis is the tool that prises the difference apart.

DuPont splits ROE into three components: net margin, asset turnover, and financial leverage (the equity multiplier). A high ROE driven by margin reflects genuine operating efficiency and is usually more durable; a high ROE driven by the equity multiplier (heavy borrowing) carries far more risk when rates rise or cash flow gets tight, even though the reported ROE looks identical.

items: ROE = Net Margin × Asset Turnover × Equity Multiplier
ROE rising mainly on the equity multiplier is a signal to check how much leverage is being carried
A high ROE is not necessarily a healthy ROE - you need to know where it came from

variables.name: Net margin
variables.description: How much profit is earned on each unit of revenue - a read on pricing power and cost control.

variables.name: Asset turnover
variables.description: How much revenue each unit of assets generates - a read on how efficiently assets are used.

variables.name: Equity multiplier
variables.description: How many times equity the assets amount to - the higher it is, the more the business leans on debt.

example.title: Two models, the same ROE
example.explanation: The same 20% ROE, but fundamentally different: one lives on turnover, the other on margin. The strategy, the risk and the way each reacts to a downturn are nothing alike.

sections.text: Reading each component's trend over five years

items: Margin drifting down: pricing power is weakening, or competition has intensified, or the product mix has shifted toward thinner-margin lines.
Asset turnover drifting down: newly invested assets have not produced matching revenue - work out whether a project is simply not at full capacity yet, or the investment was poor.
Equity multiplier drifting up: ROE is being held up by more borrowing rather than by better operations - the most worrying pattern of the three, because it masks decline in the other two.

sections.label: DuPont's final question
sections.text: Not "what is the ROE" but "if rates rise three percentage points and revenue falls 15%, which component of this ROE takes the heaviest hit". The answer tells you how durable the number in front of you really is.

lines: ROE is a composite number, not the end of the analysis.
DuPont helps you ask the right next question: where did this number come from?

practicePrompt.question: The three-part DuPont equation decomposes Return on Equity (ROE) into which ratios?
options: ROE = Margin × Turnover × Leverage
ROE = Revenue × Costs × Net profit
ROE = P/E × P/B × EPS
ROE = Total liabilities / Shareholders' equity
practicePrompt.explanation: The DuPont identity lets an analyst prise apart whether a high ROE comes from profitability (Net Margin), from how hard the asset base is worked (Asset Turnover), or from debt leverage (Equity Multiplier).
